extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics / classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining Archimedes' procedural standards for computing areas and volumes by the method of exhaustion and related limiting-sum arguments, and the corresponding Greek terminological conventions. Focuses on specific cases (sphere, paraboloid, spiral, parabola, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion using paired inscribed and circumscribed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes 'takes both an inscribed figure and a circumscribed figure in relation to the curve or surface of which he is investigating the area or the solid content, and then, as it were, compresses the two figures into one so that they coincide with one another and with the curvilinear figure to be measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove equality by showing the true quantity cannot be either greater or less than the proposed value (i.e. bound it above and below by inscribed and circumscribed approximants and then take the limit). Note: Archimedes does not explicitly phrase this as a limiting form, but the procedure is equivalent to taking limits (integration). Examples throughout: surfaces of sphere/segment, paraboloid segment, spiral, parabolic segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-of-revolution approximation by revolving equal polygon sides
rubrics_metrics.description: For a circle or segment with inscribed polygons whose equal sides AB, BC, CD,... revolve about the diameter, 'the surface described by the equal sides of the polygon in a complete revolution is ... equal to a circle with radius ...' leading to trigonometric summations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct inscribed (and circumscribed) equal-sided polygons, revolve their sides about an axis to produce surfaces that can be compared to circles; express the areas as finite trigonometric sums (e.g. sums of sin kθ) and take the limiting value as the number of sides increases (cos terms → 1) to obtain the curved surface area — equivalent to evaluating the corresponding integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume comparison via cones with base equal to revolving-sides surface
rubrics_metrics.description: For figures inscribed/circumscribed to the sphere or sector, 'its volume is equal to that of a cone with base equal to the surface of the figure and height equal to the perpendicular from the centre of the sphere on any one of the equal sides of the revolving polygon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce volumes of inscribed/circumscribed solids to volumes of cones whose base area is the (previously computed) surface and whose height is the perpendicular from the center; then apply the bounding-and-limit procedure to deduce the volume of the curved solid when the inscribed and circumscribed figures are 'compressed' into one. This shows Archimedes' volumes are obtained by a discrete-to-continuum limiting process equivalent to integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple exhaustion for ellipse via increasing inscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of an ellipse is found by the simple exhaustion of the ellipse and auxiliary circle by increasing to any desired extent the number of sides in polygons inscribed to each (no simultaneous inscribed-and-circumscribed step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequences of inscribed polygons with increasing numbers of sides to approximate the ellipse area from below (and corresponding auxiliary constructions) until difference is less than any assigned amount; this is a one-sided exhaustion method rather than the paired inscribed/circumscribed approach used elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraboloid-segment volume by summing cylinders (arithmetical partition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe and circumscribe to the segment of the paraboloid figures made up of small cylinders whose axes lie along the axis of the segment and divide it into any number of equal parts; use sums of arithmetic progression terms (h + 2h + ... + nh) and a lemma to bound the volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the axis into n equal parts of length h, form circumscribed/inscribed collections of cylinders of heights h,2h,... and compare their total volumes. Use the lemma on arithmetic sums to show bounds converge; as h→0 and n→∞ with nh fixed, the discrete sum limit equals the integral (volume expressed as ∫ y dx). Archimedes concludes (segment) = 3 (cone) in ratio form, showing equivalence with modern integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloid-segment volume via sums with quadratic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove inequalities about series of the form (a h + h^2), (a·2h + (2h)^2), ... and construct inscribed and circumscribed figures of cylinders; take limits to obtain expressions equivalent to integrals like ∫ (ax + x^2) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish algebraic bounds for the finite sums involving linear plus quadratic terms, then form cylinder-approximants and let partitions become infinitely fine. The limiting value of these sums corresponds to the definite integral representing the volume of the hyperboloid segment; Archimedes' argument gives the equivalent of performing that integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spheroid-segment volume using gnomons and rectangle-difference sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Use gnomons (differences between successive rectangles) to express the inscribed and circumscribed figures' volumes as sums; take the limit of expressions involving sums of terms like h^2, (2h)^2, ... to obtain the integral equivalent (e.g. ∫ (ax - x^2) dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate the approximants' total as a base expression minus a finite sum S_n; show S_n is bounded and tends to the appropriate continuous integral as n→∞, h→0. For the half-spheroid case, use corollaries about sums of squares to get the limit corresponding to ∫ x^2 dx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a spiral via inscribed/circumscribed similar sectors (radii in arithmetic progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumscribe and inscribe figures consisting of similar sectors of circles such that the radii are in arithmetic progression h,2h,3h,..., nh (nh = a); since similar sectors are as squares of radii, bounding inequalities on sums of squares lead to the area result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form finite-sector approximants (n sectors); use inequalities h^2 + (2h)^2 + ... bounds to show circumscribed area > target > inscribed area, and let n→∞ to obtain the limit expressible as an integral (e.g. area = (1/2)∫ r^2 dθ or as presented in the text 'area = 47 a^2' notation). Also handle partial-turn cases by taking appropriate arithmetic progressions starting at b, b+h, ... and using analogous sum inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic-segment quadrature by trapezia (mechanical solution equivalent to integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct inscribed and circumscribed figures each composed of trapezia whose parallel sides are diameters of the parabola, prove inscribed < (1/3) triangle < circumscribed, and take the limit as the trapezia become infinite in number and infinitesimally narrow to get (area of segment) = 1/3 area of triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the base repeatedly; the circumscribed figure is the sum of triangle areas with geometrically decreasing factors (1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ...), the inscribed figure gives a complementary sum. Passing to the limit yields the integral expression ∫ y dx for the parabolic segment and the well-known 1/3 relation. This demonstrates equivalence with modern definite integration methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and translation practice for Archimedean Greek geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Group Greek technical terms under general headings (points/lines, angles, planes/figures, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, etc.) and when explaining single words use ordinary Greek forms while quoting phrases from Heiberg's text (Doric or Attic) for illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing/translating Archimedes: (1) be aware that Archimedes wrote in Doric dialect but many editions transform dialects; (2) prefer ordinary (atticized) forms when explaining individual words, but quote original forms as they appear in the critical text; (3) organize terms under headings so modern equivalents are readily traceable (e.g. σημεῖον = point, γραμμή/εὐθεῖα = line, κύκλος = circle, διάμετρος = diameter, γνώμων = gnomon, δύναμις = square/power). This sets a consistent standard for producing scholarly editions and translations.
